slides.title: Values, names and references
slides.text: Session 1 Values, names and references Trace a short program line by line with a table of names and objects Predict when two names share one mutable object and when they do not Distinguish rebinding a name from mutating an object 01

slides.title: A name is a label tied to an object, not a box that holds a value
slides.text: Names and objects A name is a label tied to an object, not a box that holds a value reading = 0.742 latest = reading reading = 0.810 print(latest) # 0.742 Line 1 makes an object, 0.742, and ties the name reading to it Line 2 ties a second name to the same object Line 3 ties reading to a new object; latest is not asked Read = as "now names". The right side is worked out first; then the name on the left is tied to the result.

slides.title: Assignment never copies: b = a gives one list two names
slides.text: Aliasing Assignment never copies: b = a gives one list two names a = [1, 2, 3] b = a b.append(4) print(a, len(b)) It prints [1, 2, 3, 4] 4 There was only ever one list. append changed it, and both names show the change. What goes wrong. You "save the original" with backup = rows, clean rows, and the backup is cleaned too.

slides.title: A line either changes an object or moves a name. Know which.
slides.text: Two different things a line can do A line either changes an object or moves a name. Know which. The line What it does Who sees it b.append(4), b[0] = 9, d["k"] = 1 changes the object (mutation) every name tied to that object b = b + [4], b = [], n = n + 1 ties the name to another object (rebinding) only that name The test. Is there a bare name on the left of =? Then it is rebinding. A dot or a bracket on the left, or a method that changes in place, is mutation.

slides.title: Numbers, strings and tuples cannot change, so sharing them is harmless
slides.text: Mutable and immutable Numbers, strings and tuples cannot change, so sharing them is harmless Cannot be changed int, float, str, bool, tuple, None. Every "change" makes a new object: y = y + 5, name.upper(). Can be changed in place list, dict, set, and most objects you define. Sharing one of these is where surprises come from. x = 10 y = x y = y + 5 print(x, y) # 10 15

slides.title: A copy is one level deep: the outside is new, the inside is shared
slides.text: Copies A copy is one level deep: the outside is new, the inside is shared meter = {"id": "M-0042", "readings": [0.6]} backup = dict(meter) backup["id"] = "M-0043" backup["readings"].append(0.7) print(meter["id"], meter["readings"]) a[:], list(a), dict(d) and .copy() make a new outer object What is inside is not copied: both dictionaries point at one list of readings copy.deepcopy copies all levels, when you need it It prints M-0042 [0.6, 0.7]: the id was safe, the readings were not.

slides.title: == asks "equal value?"; is asks "the same object?"
slides.text: Two questions == asks "equal value?"; is asks "the same object?" a = [0.7, 0.9] b = a c = a[:] print(a == c, a is c) # True False print(a == b, a is b) # True True Use == for values, almost always Use is for None: if value is None When a trace surprises you, a is b tells you whether you have one object or two

slides.title: A call ties the parameter name to the caller's object: no copy there either
slides.text: Calling a function A call ties the parameter name to the caller's object: no copy there either def add_reading(log, value): log.append(value) log = [] log.append(-1) day = [1.2] add_reading(day, 0.8) print(day) call log and day name one list line 2 that list becomes [1.2, 0.8] line 3 log is tied to a new empty list line 4 the new list gets -1; nobody else sees it prints [1.2, 0.8]

slides.title: Trace on paper: a column per name, a row per line that runs
slides.text: The method Trace on paper: a column per name, a row per line that runs Line readings copy Note readings = [0.7, 0.9] list A: 0.7, 0.9 a new list, A copy = readings[:] A list B: 0.7, 0.9 a slice makes a second list copy[0] = 9.9 A B: 9.9, 0.9 mutation of B only readings.append(1.1) A: 0.7, 0.9, 1.1 B mutation of A only print(readings, copy) [0.7, 0.9, 1.1] [9.9, 0.9] Give objects letters. Two names with the same letter share an object. That is the whole trick, and it is what a step visualiser draws for you.

slides.text: Checkpoint What does the last line print? Salma keeps yesterday's readings before cleaning today's: before = rows, then rows.remove(-1.0), then rows = rows + [0.5]. The list started as [0.7, -1.0]. What is before now? [0.7, -1.0] [0.7] [0.7, 0.5] [0.7, -1.0, 0.5]

slides.title: Functions with clear contracts
slides.text: Session 2 Functions with clear contracts Split a script into functions that each do one job State a function's inputs and output in its signature and docstring Explain what a function can see and change, using scope and the call stack 02

slides.title: A forty-line script does four jobs, and you can test none of them
slides.text: Decomposition A forty-line script does four jobs, and you can test none of them 1 · Load read the file into rows → 2 · Clean keep the numbers, count the rest → 3 · Compute the amount due → 4 · Present four lines of text To check the tariff you must have a file, run everything, and read the last line A function per job gives each job a name, a way in and a way out

slides.title: Everything in comes through parameters; everything out through return
slides.text: Contracts Everything in comes through parameters; everything out through return def bill(total_m3): """Take a month's consumption in cubic metres; return the amount due in SAR.""" if total_m3 <= 15: amount = total_m3 * 2.0 else: amount = 30.0 + (total_m3 - 15) * 4.5 return amount + 5.0 The first line and the docstring are the contract: what goes in, what comes out No name from outside is read, nothing outside is changed So one line checks it: bill(15.0) == 35.0 What goes wrong. A function that prints its result returns None. The caller has nothing to work with.

slides.title: Keep files and printing at the edge, and the middle becomes easy to test
slides.text: Where the effects go Keep files and printing at the edge, and the middle becomes easy to test Edge in load_rows(path) is the only function that opens a file. The middle clean, bill, format_bill: values in, values out. The same input always gives the same output. Edge out main() is the only place that prints. You will see this shape all week. Miqyas loads at one end, writes a report at the other, and everything between is functions you can call with three rows typed by hand.

slides.title: A name bound inside a function lives inside that call, and nowhere else
slides.text: Scope A name bound inside a function lives inside that call, and nowhere else total = 0 def add(value): total = value return total add(5) print(total, add(7)) # 0 7 Assigning to total inside add makes a local name The total of line 1 is a different name in a different scope A function may read an outer name; assigning never reaches it So do not rely on outer names at all. Pass what the function needs; return what it produces.

slides.title: Every call gets its own frame of names, stacked on the caller's
slides.text: The call stack Every call gets its own frame of names, stacked on the caller's bill(17.211) total_m3, amount ↓ main() rows, values, skipped ↓ the module load_rows, clean, bill, main The top frame is the function running now When it returns, its frame and its local names are gone A traceback is this stack printed at the moment of an error, the top frame last

slides.title: A docstring states the contract; a doctest is an example that runs
slides.text: Saying the contract A docstring states the contract; a doctest is an example that runs def parse_value(text): """Turn the consumption cell into cubic metres. >>> parse_value(" 0.750 ") 0.75 >>> parse_value("12") 12.0 """ First line: what goes in, what comes out, in words Lines that start with >>> are a session someone can retype python -m doctest file.py runs them and reports any that no longer hold Examples age well. A sentence can drift from the code without anyone noticing; an example that runs cannot.

slides.title: The main guard lets a file be both a script and something to import
slides.text: Run or import The main guard lets a file be both a script and something to import def main(): rows = load_rows("data/sample_meter.csv") values, skipped = clean(rows) amount = bill(sum(values)) ... if __name__ == "__main__": main() Run the file: Python sets __name__ to "__main__", so main() runs Import the file: __name__ is "monthly_bill", nothing runs The tests import it. Without the guard, every test run would print a bill

slides.title: A default value is made once, when the function is defined
slides.text: A trap in the signature A default value is made once, when the function is defined def tag(reading, tags=[]): tags.append(reading) return tags first = tag("high") second = tag("low") print(first, second, first is second) It prints ['high', 'low'] ['high', 'low'] True def tag(reading, tags=None): if tags is None: tags = [] One list for every call. A mutable default remembers what earlier calls did. Remember this slide on Day 3.

slides.title: Which version of the function can be tested with one line?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which version of the function can be tested with one line? Shouq needs a function that counts the rows of a month with an empty consumption cell. Four colleagues propose one each. Which can be checked by a single assert, with no file on disk? count_missing() opens the month's file and returns the count count_missing(rows) prints the count count_missing(rows) returns the count count_missing(rows) stores the count in a global named missing

slides.title: Type hints and a checker
slides.text: Session 3 Type hints and a checker Annotate parameters and return values with built-in types Read a type checker's report and find the line it points at Handle a value that may be None before using it 03

slides.title: A type hint is a promise about a value, written where a tool can check it
slides.text: Type hints A type hint is a promise about a value, written where a tool can check it def parse_value(text: str) -> float | None: if text == "": return None return float(text) text: str: callers promise to pass text -> float | None: the function promises a number, or None Python itself ignores hints when it runs the code A type checker reads them and finds every line that breaks a promise

slides.title: Say what is inside: a list of what, a dictionary from what to what
slides.text: Hints for collections Say what is inside: a list of what, a dictionary from what to what Hint Reads as At Manahil list[float] a list of numbers one meter's month dict[str, int] text keys, whole-number values readings per district set[str] a set of text the known meter ids tuple[str, str, float] exactly three values, in this order meter, day, cubic metres dict[str, str] text to text one row of a CSV file The last row matters. A CSV reader gives you text for every cell, numbers included. The hint says so, and the checker stops you adding text to a number.

slides.title: "Or None" in a hint forces every caller to handle the missing case
slides.text: The value that is not there "Or None" in a hint forces every caller to handle the missing case value = parse_value(text) return meter_id, day, round(value, 3) value = parse_value(text) if value is None: return None return meter_id, day, round(value, 3) Before: an empty cell crashes at round(None, 3), some day, on some file After the check, the checker knows value is a float on the last line: this is called narrowing Not if not value. A reading of 0.0 is a real reading, and it is "not value" too.

slides.title: On code without hints, a clean report from the checker proves nothing
slides.text: From the lab's run On code without hints, a clean report from the checker proves nothing 0 issues reported on the supplied parser, while 4 of its 6 tests fail 9 errors in strict mode: every one says "missing a type annotation" 9 different errors once five signatures are annotated: each a real bug Strict mode refuses unannotated functions, so "no issues" means what it says. The labs and the capstone use mypy --strict.

slides.title: Every line of the report is a place, a complaint and a code
slides.text: Reading the report Every line of the report is a place, a complaint and a code parser.py:26: error: "None" object is not iterable [misc] parser.py:43: error: Unsupported operand types for > ("float" and "str") [operator] parser.py:45: error: Incompatible return value type (got "str", expected "float | None") [return-value] Line 26 Three names are unpacked from something that may be None. Line 43 A number is compared with text. Python would raise a TypeError here. Line 45 The function returns text where its hint promised a number.

slides.title: A checker verifies your code, not the file someone sends you
slides.text: What hints cannot do A checker verifies your code, not the file someone sends you The checker catches Text added to a number, a forgotten None, a wrong return, a misspelt field of a record: mistakes in the program. The checker cannot see A cell that holds N/A, a reading of 9,000 cubic metres, a meter that is not in the registry: mistakes in the data. Both are needed. Hints keep the code honest. Validation at the door, with a reason for every rejected row, keeps the data honest. That is Day 3.

slides.title: A type checker and a linter read your code without running it
slides.text: Two kinds of tool A type checker and a linter read your code without running it Tool Asks Examples In the workspace Type checker do the values fit the hints? mypy, Pyright uv run mypy --strict file.py Linter is anything unused, shadowed or suspicious? Ruff uv run ruff check Formatter is the layout the usual one? Ruff uv run ruff format The names are examples. An editor such as VS Code or VSCodium shows the same reports as you type. What matters is that a clean report is part of "done".

slides.title: The checker rejects this line. What is the right repair?
slides.text: Checkpoint The checker rejects this line. What is the right repair? highest(lines) is annotated -> float | None. A colleague writes peak = highest(lines) * 1.1 and the checker reports that None does not support *. Keep the result in a name, test it is None first, then multiply Add # type: ignore to the line, since the files are never empty in practice Change the hint of highest to -> float Write if not highest(lines) and return early

slides.title: Parsons problems
slides.text: Session 4 Parsons problems Order the lines of a function so that each name is bound before it is used Use indentation to say which lines belong to a branch, a loop or a try Reject a distractor by saying what it would do 04

slides.title: All the lines are given, scrambled. You decide order and indentation.
slides.text: Parsons problems All the lines are given, scrambled. You decide order and indentation. return total if value >= 0: total = value def total_valid(values): total += value for value in values: total = 0.0 No syntax to recall: every character you need is on the page What is left is the structure: what runs first, what is inside what One line is a distractor: it looks right and does not belong Why practise this. It is the skill between reading and writing, and it is one part of the supervised check.

slides.title: A line can run only after the lines that bind the names it reads
slides.text: Rule 1 A line can run only after the lines that bind the names it reads text = row[…].strip() needs row, a parameter → value = float(text) needs text → if value < 0 or value > 200: needs value For each line, list the names it reads; find the line that binds each That gives you chains like this one before you think about meaning at all Run a line too early and Python says NameError: name 'value' is not defined

slides.title: Indentation says what belongs to what, and one level changes the answer
slides.text: Rule 2 Indentation says what belongs to what, and one level changes the answer for value in values: if value >= 0: total += value return total for value in values: if value >= 0: total += value return total Left: return after the loop, the sum of all valid values Right: return inside the loop, so the function ends after the first value Both are valid Python. Only a test, or a trace, tells them apart

slides.title: Reject each bad case early; what reaches the last line is good
slides.text: The shape of a validation function Reject each bad case early; what reaches the last line is good def validate_reading(row, known): text = row["consumption_m3"].strip() if text == "": return "MISSING_VALUE" ... if row["meter_id"] not in known: return "UNKNOWN_METER" return "" Each if guards one return with one reason The order of the guards is part of the specification The final line is not indented under any if Pair them up. In a scrambled validation function, match every if with its return first. Half the puzzle is done.

slides.title: try wraps the one line that can fail; except names that failure
slides.text: Where the try goes try wraps the one line that can fail; except names that failure try: value = float(text) except ValueError: return "NOT_A_NUMBER" float("N/A") raises ValueError except TypeError: would catch nothing here: the error passes through and the function crashes except: alone would catch everything, including your own typing mistakes Name the exception you expect. You find its name by trying the failing call once and reading the last line of what Python prints.

slides.title: Decide between two lines that look alike by running one concrete row in your head
slides.text: Distractors Decide between two lines that look alike by running one concrete row in your head The row has if value < 0 or value > 200: if value < 0 and value > 200: "250" False or True: rejected False and True: accepted "-0.5" True or False: rejected True and False: accepted "0.742" accepted accepted No number is below 0 and above 200 at once. The second line never rejects anything. You see it in ten seconds with one value; you may not see it in ten minutes of staring.

slides.title: The same three questions build a function when no lines are given
slides.text: From reading to writing The same three questions build a function when no lines are given 1 · What is the contract? Inputs, output, and the cases in words. Session 2. 2 · What must exist first? The chain of names: load, then convert, then compare. Today's rule 1. 3 · What is inside what? Which lines belong to the loop, the branch, the try. Today's rule 2. From tomorrow you write. Every lab still starts from a supplied state and a set of tests that say what "right" means.

slides.title: Where does the last line of the function go?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where does the last line of the function go? A function counts the good rows. Placed so far: count = 0, the for line, the if line, count += 1. Left: return count. A test shows it returns 1 for 30 good rows. Directly under count = 0, before the loop Under count += 1, at the same depth Under the if line, at the depth of the if After the loop, at the depth of the for line

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep One object, many names Assignment and calls never copy. Mutation is seen through every name; rebinding through one. A function is a contract In through parameters, out through return, effects at the edge. Hints make the contract checkable. Give the line an input To judge a line, a distractor or a suggestion, run one concrete value through it by hand.

slides.text: Review of Day 1 One list or two? A function clean(rows) runs rows.sort() and returns rows[:10]. A caller writes top = clean(month). Afterwards, what is true of month? It is unchanged: the function worked on its own copy It is sorted, and still has all its rows It is sorted and cut to ten rows It is the same object as top

slides.title: Dictionaries for counting and grouping
slides.text: Session 1 Dictionaries for counting and grouping Count and group records with a dictionary in one pass Build an index from a key to a record and use it in place of a search Explain why a loop inside a loop is slow on 100,000 rows, and measure it 01

slides.title: A dictionary answers "what belongs to this key?" in one step
slides.text: Dictionaries A dictionary answers "what belongs to this key?" in one step district_of = { "M-0001": "Al-Rabwa", "M-0002": "Al-Yasmin", } print(district_of["M-0002"]) print("M-9001" in district_of) Each key appears once and leads to one value Looking up a key does not search: it goes straight there in asks whether a key exists, without raising an error Keys keep the order in which they were added Think "index", like the back of a book. You do not read the book to find a word; you look the word up.

slides.title: Counting: one pass, one dictionary, get with a default
slides.text: Pattern 1 Counting: one pass, one dictionary, get with a default counts: dict[str, int] = {} for reading in readings: meter_id = reading["meter_id"] counts[meter_id] = counts.get(meter_id, 0) + 1 counts.get(key, 0): the count so far, or 0 for a key not seen yet counts[key] += 1 alone raises KeyError on the first reading of a meter collections.Counter(…) is this loop, ready made On the month 588 meters have readings in the clean file; M-0001 has 30, one per day of September (lab 2.1).

slides.title: Grouping: the value is a list, and each record joins the list of its key
slides.text: Pattern 2 Grouping: the value is a list, and each record joins the list of its key by_meter: dict[str, list[float]] = {} for reading in readings: value = float(reading["consumption_m3"]) meter_id = reading["meter_id"] by_meter.setdefault(meter_id, []).append(value) setdefault(key, []) returns the list of the key, creating an empty one the first time After the loop, by_meter["M-0042"] is that meter's whole month This is how Miqyas finds each meter's median before it looks for anomalies What goes wrong. dict.fromkeys(ids, []) gives every key the same list. Yesterday's aliasing, in a dictionary.

slides.title: To combine two files, index one of them and look up from the other
slides.text: Pattern 3 To combine two files, index one of them and look up from the other 1 · Index meters.csv becomes meter id → district, once → 2 · Walk each reading, one after another → 3 · Look up the district of its meter, in one step district_of = {m["meter_id"]: m["district"] for m in meters} for reading in readings: district = district_of[reading["meter_id"]]

slides.title: The same counts, a hundred times slower: a loop inside a loop
slides.text: From the lab's run The same counts, a hundred times slower: a loop inside a loop 2.3 s nested loop: for each of 100,000 readings, search 600 meters 0.024 s dictionary: index 600 meters once, then one lookup per reading 300 comparisons per reading, on average, in the nested version It gets worse with size. Ten times the meters makes the nested version ten times slower again. The dictionary version hardly notices.

slides.title: The key itself says where its value is stored
slides.text: Why one step The key itself says where its value is stored Python turns the key into a number, its hash, and uses it as an address So finding a key costs about the same in 600 entries as in 600,000 The price: a key must never change. Text, numbers and tuples can be keys; lists and dictionaries cannot >>> {["M-0001", "2026-09-01"]: 0.7} TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' >>> {("M-0001", "2026-09-01"): 0.7} {('M-0001', '2026-09-01'): 0.7}

slides.title: Three ways to ask for a key, and they fail differently on purpose

slides.title: A set drops repeats and forgets order: sort before you show it
slides.text: What a set gives up A set drops repeats and forgets order: sort before you show it >>> ids = ["M-0002", "M-0001", "M-0002"] >>> set(ids) {'M-0002', 'M-0001'} >>> sorted(set(ids)) ['M-0001', 'M-0002'] set(a_list) is the shortest way to drop repeats The order you see printed is not promised, and can differ between runs sorted(…) turns any collection into a list in a fixed order A report must be the same on two runs. slides.title: Finding repeats: remember what you have seen, as a set of tuples
slides.text: Pattern Finding repeats: remember what you have seen, as a set of tuples seen: set[tuple[str, str]] = set() repeated: set[tuple[str, str]] = set() for reading in readings: key = (reading["meter_id"], reading["date"]) if key in seen: repeated.add(key) seen.add(key) The identity of a reading is the pair: this meter, this date A tuple cannot change, so it can be a member of a set set() makes an empty set; {} is an empty dictionary On the month 30 pairs appear more than once. Miqyas keeps the first row of each and rejects the repeat as DUPLICATE.

slides.title: A comprehension builds a collection in one expression: what, from where, which
slides.text: Comprehensions A comprehension builds a collection in one expression: what, from where, which values = [float(r["consumption_m3"]) for r in rows] # a list high = [v for v in values if v > 5.0] # with a filter known = {m["meter_id"] for m in meters} # a set district_of = {m["meter_id"]: m["district"] for m in meters} # a dictionary What The expression at the front: one item of the result. From where for … in …: the same line as in a loop. Which An optional if at the end keeps only some.

slides.title: One expression and one condition fit a comprehension; anything more wants a loop
slides.text: Judgement One expression and one condition fit a comprehension; anything more wants a loop Comprehension Transform each item, or keep some. The reader sees the whole idea on one line. Loop Counting and grouping, a try around each item, two results at once, an early exit, or a line that no longer fits on the screen. ok = [float(r["consumption_m3"]) for r in rows if r["consumption_m3"].strip() != "" and r["meter_id"] in known and 0 <= float(r["consumption_m3"]) <= 200] What goes wrong. The line above converts twice, crashes on N/A, and cannot say why a row was left out.

slides.title: A function with yield hands over one value, then waits to be asked again
slides.text: Generators A function with yield hands over one value, then waits to be asked again def read_values(path): with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as file: for row in csv.DictReader(file): yield float(row["consumption_m3"]) return ends a function; yield pauses it, with all its names kept The next request resumes it on the line after the yield At any moment, one row exists. The file stays open until the loop is done

slides.title: Calling a generator function runs nothing: the work happens when values are asked for
slides.text: Laziness Calling a generator function runs nothing: the work happens when values are asked for call values = read_values("data/readings_large.csv") no file is opened yet next(values) opens the file, reads one row, gives 0.606 and pauses next(values) reads one more row, gives 0.544 and pauses sum(values) asks again and again until the file ends: the total of everything left for and sum ask for you. You rarely write next; every loop over a generator is this conversation.

slides.title: The same total of 100,000 rows, with two hundred times less memory
slides.text: From the lab's run The same total of 100,000 rows, with two hundred times less memory List of all rows 35,900 KiB Stream, one row at a time 160 KiB Both give 137,769.165 cubic metres A file ten times as long: the list needs ten times the memory, the stream the same 160 KiB A year of every meter's hourly readings does not fit in a list on a laptop. It does fit in a stream

slides.title: A generator can be walked once. Then it is empty.
slides.text: The price A generator can be walked once. Then it is empty. >>> values = read_values(path) >>> sum(values) 137769.165 >>> sum(values) 0 >>> len(values) TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len() No length, no positions, no second pass Need two results? Compute both in one loop, or call the function again for a fresh generator Need to sort, or to find a median? You need all the values: use a list The silent zero. A second pass does not raise an error. It quietly gives the result for no data.

slides.title: Round brackets make a comprehension lazy
slides.text: The short form Round brackets make a comprehension lazy total = sum([float(r["consumption_m3"]) for r in rows]) total = sum(float(r["consumption_m3"]) for r in rows) First: build a list of 100,000 numbers, add them, throw the list away Second: hand each number to sum as it is made Works with sum, max, min, any, all, sorted, set

slides.text: Records A dictionary as a record accepts any mistake until the line that uses it ticket = json.loads(line) ticket["priorty"] = "urgent" if ticket["opened"] < "2026-09-01": ... Line 2 misspells the field and adds a new key. No error, ever Line 3 compares dates as text. It works only while every file writes year-month-day Nothing says which fields a ticket has, or what type each is The checker sees dict[str, str] and can help with none of it

slides.title: A data class is a record with named, typed fields, written in six lines
slides.text: Data classes A data class is a record with named, typed fields, written in six lines @dataclass(frozen=True) class Ticket: ticket_id: str opened: date district: str priority: str status: str text: str The decorator writes the constructor, a readable printout and == for you Ticket(ticket_id="T-20001", opened=…) builds one; t.priority reads a field A misspelt field is an AttributeError at run time and an error from the checker before

slides.title: frozen=True makes a record that nobody can change behind your back
slides.text: Frozen frozen=True makes a record that nobody can change behind your back >>> t.priority = "low" dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'priority' >>> urgent = replace(t, priority="urgent") Yesterday: a shared mutable object changes for every name that holds it A frozen record can be shared freely: there is nothing to mutate A "change" makes a new record with dataclasses.replace, like upper() on a string Frozen records can be keys of a dictionary and members of a set

slides.title: A method is a function that lives with the data it needs
slides.text: Behaviour that belongs to the record A method is a function that lives with the data it needs def age_days(self, today: date) -> int: """Whole days from the day the ticket was opened to today.""" return (today - self.opened).days self is the record the method was called on: t.age_days(today) today comes in as a parameter. A method that asked the clock would give a different answer tomorrow, and could not be tested opened is a date, so subtraction gives days. As text it would give an error On the queue The oldest open urgent ticket, T-20087, is 41 days old on the course's "today", 1 October 2026 (lab 2.4).

slides.title: sorted needs to know what to compare: give it a key function
slides.text: Sorting sorted needs to know what to compare: give it a key function RANK = {"urgent": 0, "high": 1, "normal": 2, "low": 3} by_text = sorted(tickets, key=lambda t: t.priority) by_rank = sorted(tickets, key=lambda t: RANK[t.priority]) The key function is called once per item; items are ordered by what it returns By text: high, low, normal, urgent. Alphabetical, and useless By rank: urgent first, because 0 is the smallest lambda t: … is a function small enough to write in place

slides.title: A key that returns a tuple sorts by the first item, then the second, then the third
slides.text: Sorting by several fields A key that returns a tuple sorts by the first item, then the second, then the third sorted(waiting, key=lambda t: (PRIORITY_RANK[t.priority], t.opened, t.ticket_id)) Ticket Rank Opened Age in days District T-20087 0 urgent 2026-08-21 41 Al-Yasmin T-20274 0 urgent 2026-08-24 38 Al-Naseem T-20066 0 urgent 2026-08-25 37 Al-Khuzama T-20196 0 urgent 2026-08-26 36 Al-Naseem The last item breaks ties. Two urgent tickets of the same day would otherwise come out in file order; the ticket id makes the queue the same on every run.

slides.title: A record carries only the fields the task needs
slides.text: Responsible use A record carries only the fields the task needs In the file Ten fields per ticket, among them a phone number and an identity number: personal data. In Ticket Six fields. The queue is ordered by priority and age; it needs to call nobody and identify nobody. What is never copied into the record cannot be printed, logged or written by mistake The free text of a ticket can hold a phone number too. Tomorrow's first lab masks it before anything is written The data here is synthetic. The habit is real: Abdulaziz, the data protection officer, reads your output files, not your intentions.

slides.title: Three things to say every time you open a text file
slides.text: Opening a file Three things to say every time you open a text file with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as file: rows = list(csv.DictReader(file)) with: the file is closed when the block ends, also when an error happens inside it encoding="utf-8": you decide how bytes become text, not the machine you happen to be on newline="": for CSV, let the csv module handle line ends, so that a line break inside a quoted cell survives What goes wrong. Leave the encoding out and the same script reads Arabic on one laptop and crashes on the next. Session 2 shows it.

slides.title: A CSV reader hands you text for every cell. Numbers and dates are your job.
slides.text: CSV A CSV reader hands you text for every cell. Numbers and dates are your job. >>> row = rows[0] >>> row {'meter_id': 'M-0001', 'date': '2026-09-01', 'consumption_m3': '5.399'} >>> row["consumption_m3"] * 2 '5.3995.399' csv.DictReader uses the header line as keys: one dict[str, str] per row CSV has no types. '5.399' is five characters until you call float Convert in one place, at the door, and reject there what will not convert

slides.title: A comma inside a cell is why line.split(",") is not a CSV reader
slides.text: Why a module, not split A comma inside a cell is why line.split(",") is not a CSV reader meter_id,date,consumption_m3 M-0001,2026-09-01,5.399 M-0580,2026-09-01,"0,361" Third row gives line.split(",") four pieces: "0 and 361" apart csv.DictReader three cells; the value is 0,361 A spreadsheet set to a comma as the decimal mark writes numbers this way, in quotes The month file has 7 such cells. The reader gets them whole; float then refuses them, and they are rejected as NOT_A_NUMBER with the text in the detail

slides.title: JSON Lines is one JSON value per line: a file you can read one record at a time
slides.text: JSON Lines JSON Lines is one JSON value per line: a file you can read one record at a time with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file: for line in file: ticket = json.loads(line) Each line stands alone: a broken line spoils one record, not the file Records can be appended, and streamed with a generator Unlike CSV, a value has a type: text, number, true or false, null, list, object At Manahil Each of the 400 tickets is one line with ten fields. The free text is Arabic, English or both in one sentence.

slides.title: Write output that is the same bytes on every run, and that a person can read
slides.text: Writing Write output that is the same bytes on every run, and that a person can read with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as file: json.dump(summary, file, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) file.write("\n") ensure_ascii=False: Arabic is written as Arabic, not as escapes such as ا indent=2: one field per line, so that two versions can be compared Keys in a fixed order: build the dictionary from sorted names No clock time inside the file: put that in the log Same input, same bytes. Then "did anything change?" is answered by comparing two files, and Day 4's tool can prove it reruns.

slides.title: A file holds bytes. Text appears only when an encoding is applied.
slides.text: Bytes and text A file holds bytes. Text appears only when an encoding is applied. The word عداد (meter) Bytes in UTF-8 d8 b9 d8 af d8 a7 d8 af in Windows-1256 da cf c7 cf Text (str) is a sequence of characters: 4 here Bytes are numbers from 0 to 255: 8 here, or 4 An encoding is the table between the two. encode goes to bytes, decode comes back The bytes do not say which table wrote them. Someone has to tell you, or you have to find out.

slides.title: UTF-8 covers every script and is the encoding to write, always
slides.text: UTF-8 UTF-8 covers every script and is the encoding to write, always One byte English letters, digits, punctuation: the same bytes as ASCII. M-0042 is six bytes. Two bytes Each Arabic letter. The letter ف is d9 81. Not every byte order is valid A decoder can tell when bytes are not UTF-8. That is a feature: wrong input fails loudly. Older systems wrote one byte per Arabic letter (Windows-1256). Their files are still arriving Read what you are given, with the encoding it was written in. Write UTF-8

slides.title: open(path) without an encoding uses whatever the machine prefers
slides.text: The trap open(path) without an encoding uses whatever the machine prefers with open(path) as file: # which encoding? return [json.loads(line) for line in file] On many Windows laptops the default is a one-byte Western table (cp1252) On most servers and in notebooks in the cloud it is UTF-8 So the same script works in one place and fails in the other, on the same file This is changing. PEP 686 makes UTF-8 the default from Python 3.15. Until every machine you meet runs it, and for every file that is not UTF-8, name the encoding.

slides.title: A decode error names the codec, the byte and the position. Use all three.
slides.text: Reading the error A decode error names the codec, the byte and the position. Use all three. UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x81 in position 131: character maps to <undefined> The codec "charmap": a one-byte table was decoding. Nobody chose it; it was the default. The byte 0x81 has no character in that table. In UTF-8 it is the second half of ف. The position Byte 131 of what was being decoded: where to look in the file.

slides.title: The wrong one-byte table raises nothing and gives you the wrong text
slides.text: The quiet failure The wrong one-byte table raises nothing and gives you the wrong text The UTF-8 bytes of عداد, decoded as Result Error? UTF-8 عداد no Windows-1256 ط¹ط¯ط§ط¯ no cp1252, errors replaced Ø¹Ø¯Ø§Ø¯ no "It opened without an error" is not "it was decoded correctly". Text like the second and third rows, in a report or a database, means a file was read with the wrong table somewhere upstream.

slides.title: errors="ignore" makes the error go away by deleting the customer's words
slides.text: The tempting repair errors="ignore" makes the error go away by deleting the customer's words Line 12 of the branch file, decoded as UTF-8 with The text of the ticket becomes errors="strict" (the default) a UnicodeDecodeError: you are told errors="ignore" a few spaces, one stray letter and M-0365 errors="replace" rows of � marks and M-0365 the encoding it was written in (Windows-1256) الفاتورة مرتفعة جدا هذا الشهر، أرجو مراجعة قراءة العداد M-0365 Fail loudly, then report. Decode strictly, catch the error per line, and list the lines that fail with the byte that stopped you. Then someone can decide.

slides.title: A program can meet a bad record in three ways. Only one is acceptable.
slides.text: Bad input A program can meet a bad record in three ways. Only one is acceptable. Crash Line 37 is broken, so nobody gets the other 434. And tomorrow, line 52. Pass silently Skip it, or fill in a default. The report looks complete and is wrong by an unknown amount. Reject with a reason The run finishes, the good records are used, and each bad one is listed with where and why. The rule of the house. Accepted plus rejected equals the lines of the input. Always, and checked by the program itself.

slides.title: An exception travels up the call stack until some caller catches it
slides.text: Exceptions An exception travels up the call stack until some caller catches it parse_value("N/A") raises ValueError ↓ parse_row(row) no handler: passes it on ↓ load_readings(path) has try and except: handles it, goes on raise stops the function at once; nothing is returned Each caller in turn either handles it or is stopped too If nobody handles it, the program ends and prints the stack: the traceback So the place that detects a problem need not be the place that decides what to do

slides.title: Catch the exception you expect, by name. A wide net catches your own mistakes too.
slides.text: Catching Catch the exception you expect, by name. A wide net catches your own mistakes too. try: value = flaot(text) except Exception: skipped += 1 try: value = float(text) except ValueError: skipped += 1 Left: the misspelt flaot raises a NameError on every row. The net catches it, and the script reports that all 17,690 rows were "skipped" Right: only "this text is not a number" is handled. Anything else still stops the run and shows you where A bare except: is the widest net of all. The labs' checks refuse it.

slides.title: An exception of your own can carry what the handler needs: a code and a detail
slides.text: Your own exception An exception of your own can carry what the handler needs: a code and a detail class Rejected(Exception): def __init__(self, reason, detail): super().__init__(f"{reason}: {detail}") self.reason = reason self.detail = detail raise Rejected("BAD_PRIORITY", f"priority is {value!r}") A reason code for programs: it can be counted, grouped and tested A detail for people: the actual value, so that someone can repair the line The handler catches Rejected and nothing else: every other exception is a bug to see

slides.title: Day 1's guard clauses, with raise in place of return
slides.text: Validation as guards Day 1's guard clauses, with raise in place of return if ticket["priority"] not in PRIORITIES: raise Rejected("BAD_PRIORITY", ...) try: date.fromisoformat(ticket["opened"]) except ValueError: raise Rejected("BAD_DATE", ...) from None return ticket The function now returns only good tickets. A caller cannot forget to look at a reason Let the library judge: fromisoformat knows that September has 30 days Translate its ValueError into your own exception, with your own code The first guard that fires wins: one reason per line

slides.title: The try wraps one call for one line, and the loop goes on
slides.text: The loop The try wraps one call for one line, and the loop goes on for line_no, line in enumerate(file, start=1): try: accepted.append(parse_ticket(line)) except Rejected as problem: rejected.append((line_no, problem.reason, problem.detail)) Inside the loop: one bad line costs one line A try around the whole loop would end at the first rejection and lose every line after it The line number is counted here, where it is known, and stored with the reason You wrote this shape an hour ago. Decode each line, catch the decode error, collect the failure: the same loop with another exception.

slides.title: 435 lines in: 400 accepted, 35 rejected, 0 unaccounted for
slides.text: From the lab's run 435 lines in: 400 accepted, 35 rejected, 0 unaccounted for Reason Lines MISSING_FIELD 8 BAD_JSON 6 BAD_PRIORITY 5 BAD_DATE, BAD_METER_ID 4 + 4 EMPTY_LINE, EMPTY_TEXT 3 + 3 NOT_OBJECT 2 assert len(accepted) + len(rejected) == lines The program checks its own accounting on every run The table tells the sender what to fix first The log, rejections.csv, says which line and what was in it

slides.title: The log says 435 rejected and 0 accepted. Why?
slides.text: Checkpoint The log says 435 rejected and 0 accepted. Why? A colleague's intake finishes without a crash. Every line is in the rejection log with the reason UNKNOWN. The loop reads: try: accepted.append(parse_tiket(line)), then except Exception: rejected.append((line_no, "UNKNOWN", "")). Every line of the file is malformed A typo raises NameError on every line; the wide except logs it The try is inside the loop and should be around it The file was opened with the wrong encoding

slides.text: Session 4 A debugging method Read a traceback from its last line upward Shrink a failing input to the smallest one that still fails Write a regression test that fails on the defect and passes on the fix 04

slides.title: Six steps turn "it gives wrong numbers" into a fix that stays fixed
slides.text: A method, not a talent Six steps turn "it gives wrong numbers" into a fix that stays fixed 1 · Reproduce One command that shows the wrong result, every time. 2 · Shrink The smallest input that still shows it. 3 · Hypothesis One sentence: "I think … because …". 4 · Test it An observation that would prove you wrong. 5 · Fix The smallest change, at the cause. 6 · Regression check A test that fails without the fix.

slides.title: Read a traceback from its last line upward
slides.text: When it crashes Read a traceback from its last line upward Traceback (most recent call last): File "drill.py", line 22, in <module> print(total(rows)) File "drill.py", line 17, in total result += to_number(row["consumption_m3"]) File "drill.py", line 11, in to_number return float(text) ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'N/A' Last line What went wrong, and with which value. The frame above it Where : file, line, function. The frames further up How we got there : who called whom.

slides.title: The harder defects raise nothing: they give a wrong answer politely
slides.text: When it does not crash The harder defects raise nothing: they give a wrong answer politely Report A The same file, read twice in one job. Run 1: 17,561 accepted. Run 2: 0 accepted. Report B The report gives a median of 0.653 for meter M-0012. Sorted by hand, it is 0.696. No traceback to read. You start from a difference: what you got against what must be true So step 1 is to make that difference appear on demand, with one command And somebody has to know what "must be true" is: here, the operator and Salma

slides.title: Shrink until the failing case fits in your head
slides.text: Step 2 Shrink until the failing case fits in your head 17,690 rows fails, and tells you nothing → Half of them still fails? Halve again → 2 rows, or 3 values fails, and you can check it by hand Shrink the data (fewer rows, one meter), the steps (one function, not the whole tool) and the calls (does it need two?) Each cut either keeps the failure, so you continue, or loses it, and then you have learnt what matters The smallest failing case is the regression test, almost written

slides.title: Say what you think is wrong before you touch the code, then try to prove yourself wrong
slides.text: Steps 3 and 4 Say what you think is wrong before you touch the code, then try to prove yourself wrong A hypothesis "I think the count is wrong because line 40 of report.py starts the total at 1." A file, a line, a reason. A test of it "If so, a file of one row gives 2." Run it. One row gives 1: the hypothesis is dead, in thirty seconds, with no code changed. print("start:", len(seen)) # the quick look breakpoint() # or stop here, then: # p name print a name # n next line # s step into a call # c continue q quit

slides.title: A regression test fails on the defect and passes on the fix. Then it stays.
slides.text: Step 6 A regression test fails on the defect and passes on the fix. Then it stays. def test_total_of_one_row(): rows = [{"consumption_m3": "0.5"}] assert total(rows) == 0.5 Write it from the shrunk case, before or right after the fix See it fail on the old code. A test you never saw fail may be testing nothing See it pass on the new code Keep it: it runs with every later change, for as long as the code lives The lab's check does step 2 of that list for you. It puts each defect back into a copy of the package and expects your test to fail there.

slides.title: What notebooks hide
slides.text: Session 1 What notebooks hide Read the execution counts of a saved notebook and say in which order it was run Find a name that only the kernel remembers and an output that the code on screen does not produce Choose a notebook, a script or a module for a task, with a one-line reason 01

slides.title: A notebook is two things: a page that is saved and a memory that is not
slides.text: Notebooks A notebook is two things: a page that is saved and a memory that is not The page Cells of code and text, and under each code cell the output of the last time it ran. This is the file, analysis.ipynb. It is what you send to a colleague. The kernel A running Python that holds every name any cell has bound since it started. It lives on your laptop only, and ends when you close it. What goes wrong. The page and the kernel can disagree, and nothing on the screen says so. Every problem of this session is one form of that sentence.

slides.title: The number in brackets is the order of running, not the order on the page
slides.text: Reading a saved notebook The number in brackets is the order of running, not the order on the page Cell, top to bottom Count Load the two files [1] Keep the valid readings [3] Set the factor to 3.0 [4] Find the anomalies [8] Count per district [9] What if: set the factor to 2.0 [7] A gap (no 2, no 5, no 6): a cell was run and deleted, or run again later A step backwards (9, then 7): the cell below ran before the cells above it Counts 1, 2, 3 and on: the page was run once, top to bottom

slides.title: A deleted cell leaves its names behind in the kernel
slides.text: Hidden state, first form A deleted cell leaves its names behind in the kernel known = set(district_of) if row["meter_id"] not in known: continue For Salma the notebook works: her kernel still holds known For anyone else, and for her after a restart: NameError: name 'known' is not defined The file she sent does not contain the code that produced its own outputs

slides.title: An output can be older, or newer, than the code printed above it
slides.text: Hidden state, second form An output can be older, or newer, than the code printed above it factor = 3.0 anomalies = [...] # above factor * median print(len(anomalies), "anomalies") # 27 anomalies 27 on the page, under "factor = 3.0" 18 on a clean run from top to bottom What happened. A cell further down set factor = 2.0, and the anomaly cell was run again afterwards. The 27 is true of a factor nobody can see beside it.

slides.title: Restart and run all, then read the numbers
slides.text: The one habit Restart and run all, then read the numbers Restart empties the kernel: every name is gone Run all runs the page in the order a reader sees it If it stops, the page depended on something it does not hold If a number changes, the old one was stale Then save: counts 1, 2, 3 and on tell the next reader it was done And one rule of writing Set each name in one cell. A second question gets a second name: strict_factor, not factor again. Then no cell can change what an earlier cell means.

slides.title: Three homes for code, each good at one thing
slides.text: Where code lives Three homes for code, each good at one thing Notebook For looking: a question asked once, steps you want to see, results and notes on one page. State persists between cells. Script For repeating: the same steps on new files, by anyone, with one command. Starts empty every run. Module For sharing: functions that other code imports, written once and tested in one place. Runs nothing by itself. They work together. A notebook that imports a tested module is a good notebook. Tomorrow's capstone is a script on top of modules.

slides.title: Four questions decide the home
slides.text: Choosing Four questions decide the home Ask If yes Is the way to the answer still unknown, and asked once? Notebook Will a person read the outputs and notes together, as a page? Notebook Will it run again, on new input, by someone else or by a schedule? Script Does more than one program, or a test, need the same piece? Module The usual journey. Explore in a notebook, move what survives into functions in a module, and give the routine run to a script. Session 2 makes that move.

slides.title: Which home for this task?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which home for this task? Every Sunday the branch offices send a ticket file. It must be decoded, checked and turned into a rejection log before the customer care team starts work. Nobody watches it run. A notebook that the analyst on duty opens and runs each Sunday A module with the decoding and checking functions, and nothing else A script with one command, built on functions that live in a module A notebook, because the outputs stay visible under each cell

slides.title: Scripts, modules and an entry point
slides.text: Session 2 Scripts, modules and an entry point Explain what runs when a file is imported and when it is run, and what an entry point is for Write a command line with required arguments, a default and a useful exit code Produce a report that is byte for byte the same on two runs over the same files 02

slides.title: Each cell becomes a function. What is left is the order, and that is main.
slides.text: From notebook to tool Each cell becomes a function. What is left is the order, and that is main. In the notebook In the package The cell that reads the registry load_meters(path) The cell that keeps valid readings load_readings(path, known) The cell that finds anomalies find_anomalies(readings, factor) The cells that print tables render(...), which returns text File names typed into cells arguments of the command line You, pressing run in order main() What changed. Names that lived in the kernel are now arguments and return values. Nothing is remembered between runs.

slides.title: Importing a file runs its top level. So the top level should only define things.
slides.text: One file, two uses Importing a file runs its top level. So the top level should only define things. def build_report(path): ... def main(): print(build_report("readings.csv")) if __name__ == "__main__": main() python report_tool.py: the file is the program, __name__ is "__main__", and main() runs import report_tool: the same lines run, __name__ is "report_tool", and nothing is called So a test can import build_report without starting the tool

slides.title: An entry point is the one door through which the tool is started
slides.text: A package as a program An entry point is the one door through which the tool is started miqyas/ __init__.py __main__.py the door cli.py arguments and main() readings.py load and validate anomalies.py the rule report.py aggregate and render from miqyas.cli import main raise SystemExit(main()) python -m miqyas runs __main__.py main() returns a number, and SystemExit hands it to the system as the exit code

slides.title: Arguments replace the file names typed into cells
slides.text: argparse Arguments replace the file names typed into cells report.add_argument("--readings", type=Path, required=True, help="the readings file (CSV)") report.add_argument("--factor", type=float, default=3.0, help="anomaly threshold, times the median") Converted type= turns the text of the command line into a path or a float, or refuses it with a message. Required or default An input is required. A setting has a default that is written down once. Documented --help is built from these calls: the usage text cannot drift from the code.

slides.title: The exit code is how a tool tells a schedule whether it worked
slides.text: Speaking to other programs The exit code is how a tool tells a schedule whether it worked Code Meaning in Miqyas 0 The report was written 2 An input file is missing, or the arguments are wrong 1 Something unexpected: Python ended with a traceback Zero means success; anything else means "do not use the output" A missing file is expected trouble: one clear line and code 2, not a traceback Rejected rows are not a failure: the report counts them, and the code is still 0

slides.title: The result goes to the file. What happened on the way goes to the log.
slides.text: Messages The result goes to the file. What happened on the way goes to the log. log = logging.getLogger("miqyas") log.info("%d rows accepted, %d rejected", len(readings), len(rejections)) log.error("no such file: %s", path) A level on every message: with -v you see the steps, without it only problems Log messages go to the error stream, so the output of the tool stays clean Counts and file names belong in a log. A customer's phone number or ticket text does not Personal data. A log is copied, mailed and kept for years. Yesterday's rule holds here: mask before anything is written, printed or logged.

slides.title: Same files in, same bytes out: a property you can test
slides.text: Reproducibility Same files in, same bytes out: a property you can test No time of the run in the report: the time goes in the log A fixed order everywhere: sorted districts, anomalies by meter and day The encoding and the line ends are named when writing Nothing remembered between runs: no kernel, no default that grows python -m miqyas report ... --out a.md python -m miqyas report ... --out b.md # then compare the bytes of a.md and b.md Why it matters. When the report changes next month, you know the input changed, or the code did. Without this property you know nothing.

slides.title: The test run prints a report. Why?
slides.text: Checkpoint The test run prints a report. Why? A colleague's file monthly.py defines three functions and ends with the line main(). A test file starts with from monthly import clean. Running the tests reads the month file and prints the whole report before any test starts. pytest calls every function it finds in an imported file Importing runs the file's top level, and the call of main() is at the top level Importing clean also imports main, and imported functions run once The file has no __main__.py beside it

slides.title: Tests as a safety net
slides.text: Session 3 Tests as a safety net Write a test as an arranged input, one call and an asserted result Choose examples at the boundary, for empty input and for each argument of a rule Judge a set of tests by the wrong versions of the code it would catch 03

slides.title: A test is an example with a verdict
slides.text: Tests A test is an example with a verdict >>> is_anomaly(5.0, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) True def test_far_above_is_an_anomaly(): assert is_anomaly(5.0, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) is True You have run examples at the prompt all week and judged the answers by eye A test keeps the example and the expected answer, so a machine can judge it again uv run pytest finds the functions named test_, runs each, and reports the ones whose assert was false

slides.title: Arrange, act, assert: three parts, one reason to fail
slides.text: The shape of a test Arrange, act, assert: three parts, one reason to fail def test_exactly_three_times_is_not_an_anomaly(): history = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # arrange result = is_anomaly(3.0, history) # act assert result is False # assert Arrange an input small enough to check in your head Act with one call of the thing under test Assert one fact about the result The name is the sentence the test proves: it is what a colleague reads when it fails

slides.title: Mistakes live at the edges, so that is where the examples go
slides.text: Choosing examples Mistakes live at the edges, so that is where the examples go The boundary Exactly three times the median, and just above it. > and >= differ at one point only. Nothing An empty history. What should happen is a decision; the docstring states it and a test holds it. Each argument If changing factor changes no test's answer, no test would notice that it is ignored. A way to find them. Read the docstring and the signature. Every promise and every argument deserves an example that would fail if it were broken.

slides.title: A good example gives different answers for the right rule and a wrong one
slides.text: An example that discriminates A good example gives different answers for the right rule and a wrong one History Median Mean 1, 1, 1 1.0 1.0 1, 1, 1, 1, 10 1.0 2.8 With the first history, a rule built on the mean passes every test you write With the second, the value 3.5 is an anomaly by the median (above 3.0) and not by the mean (below 8.4) One example, chosen so that the two rules disagree

slides.title: Passing tests prove the examples, not the program
slides.text: What a green run means Passing tests prove the examples, not the program What you know On these inputs the code gives these answers, today and after every change, checked in a second. What you do not know Anything about inputs nobody thought of. Defect B of yesterday passed every test that used a sorted list. Tests and types catch different mistakes: a type checker never runs the code, a test never sees the lines it does not reach A test that cannot fail is worse than none: it reports safety that is not there

slides.title: A failing test is a traceback with the values filled in
slides.text: Reading the output A failing test is a traceback with the values filled in def test_exactly_three_times_is_not_an_anomaly(): history = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] result = is_anomaly(3.0, history) > assert result is False E assert True is False test_anomalies.py:14: AssertionError 1 failed, 6 passed in 0.03s Read from the bottom, as yesterday: how many failed, which file and line, then the line marked > The E line shows what the assert compared: it expected False and got True Reproduce and shrink are already done: the test is the small failing case

slides.title: Tests are what lets you, or an assistant, change code without fear
slides.text: Why keep them Tests are what lets you, or an assistant, change code without fear Tests pass the rule is pinned down → Change the code by hand or with an assistant → Run the tests a second, every time → Still pass? keep the change, or undo it The sixth step of debugging adds one test per defect, so the net grows where the code has failed before Code an assistant wrote for you is code you have not read line by line. Your tests are how you hold it to the rule

slides.title: Which test would catch it?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which test would catch it? Someone "tidies" the rule and writes value >= factor * median(history) where it said >. Which test fails? The value 5.0 with the history 1, 1, 1 is an anomaly The value 1.1 with the history 1, 1, 1 is not an anomaly The value 100.0 with an empty history is not an anomaly The value 3.0 with the history 1, 1, 1 is not an anomaly

slides.text: The question of the week An assistant can write this week's code in seconds. So what did you learn it for? Someone has to say whether the code is right. This week that was you, sixteen times Reading, tracing and debugging are the skills that judging needs The defects of labs 3.4 and 4.4 run without an error and print plausible numbers The claim of this session An assistant changes how you produce code. Whether it also changes what you learn depends on how you use it, and there is evidence on that.

slides.title: Learning a new library with an assistant: the task got done, less of it stayed
slides.text: A randomised experiment, 2026 Learning a new library with an assistant: the task got done, less of it stayed 67% average quiz score, coding by hand 50% average quiz score, coding with an AI assistant Developers learnt a Python library they had not used, half with an assistant and half without Afterwards everyone took the same quiz on the library, without help The study comes from a company that builds assistants, and reports a cost of using them Source: Anthropic, "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills" (2026), arXiv 2601.20245.

slides.title: The largest gap was on debugging questions
slides.text: The same study The largest gap was on debugging questions The quiz asked about concepts, reading code and debugging The group that used the assistant fell behind most where it had to find what was wrong in code That is the skill needed to check what an assistant hands you Why this course does what it does Daily drills on paper. The first attempt at each debugging lab alone. A supervised check without an assistant. A capstone you walk through and change live.

slides.title: How people used the assistant mattered, not only whether
slides.text: The same study How people used the assistant mattered, not only whether Handing the work over Ask for the code, paste it, ask again when it fails. The task is finished and the reasoning was never yours. Keeping the thinking Ask why, ask for an explanation with the code, ask about the idea and write the code yourself. Participants who worked this way kept more. So the choice is yours each time. The same tool can be an answer machine or a tutor. Which one it is depends on what you ask it for.

slides.title: Attempt first, ask for a hint, explain it back
slides.text: A way of working while you learn Attempt first, ask for a hint, explain it back 1 · Attempt reproduce, shrink, a first hypothesis, in writing → 2 · Hint one at a time; do what it says before the next → 3 · Explain assistant closed, in your words, no code The attempt gives the hint something to attach to. Without it, a hint is an answer in slow motion The explanation is the test of whether you learnt it. If you cannot write it, you have a fix and not yet an understanding

slides.title: A question that gets a hint says what you expected, what you saw and what you tried
slides.text: Asking well A question that gets a hint says what you expected, what you saw and what you tried Gets an answer to paste "Here is report.py. The district counts are wrong. Fix it." Gets a hint to use "Every district shows 18 and I expected different counts. With two meters and one anomaly both districts show it. I think the lists are shared. Do not give me code: what should I check to prove it?" The course tutor, Dalil. It is instructed to give one hint at a time and no code, and the workspace's agent instructions ask the same of any assistant opened there.

slides.title: What you send to a hosted assistant has left the organisation
slides.text: Before you paste What you send to a hosted assistant has left the organisation Code you wrote for a lab: fine. A traceback: read it first, it may quote a record A customer's ticket, phone number or meter history: personal data, not to be sent to a service your organisation has not approved Shrink first. A case built by hand with two invented meters shows the defect and holds nobody's data In this lab The tutor sends your question and the source files you name. It refuses anything under data/. The data here is synthetic; the habit is for the day it is not.

slides.title: Three modes, each with a reason
slides.text: How this course uses assistants Three modes, each with a reason Off The daily drills, the first attempt at labs 3.4 and 4.4, and the supervised check: tracing on paper and one debugging task in a locked editor. Tutor The other labs: an assistant may give hints and explain, and is told not to give code. Full The capstone: any tool you like. Then you run it, change it on request and read a traceback from it, live. What all three protect. That the person who signs the work can explain it.

slides.title: What do you do next?
slides.text: Checkpoint What do you do next? You are learning. A report shows the same count for every district. You have reproduced it and have no idea yet where it comes from. An assistant is open in the next window. Paste the package and ask for the corrected file Paste the package and ask which line is wrong, then fix it yourself Shrink it to a case built by hand, write a first guess, then ask for one hint on what to check Close the assistant and never use it for debugging

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 4 · wrap-up Three things to keep Restart and run all A notebook's page and its kernel can disagree. Read numbers only after a clean run, and move what repeats into a script on modules. One command, same bytes Arguments, an exit code, a log, and tests at the edges of the rule. That is a tool someone else can trust. Attempt, hint, explain Use an assistant so that the reasoning stays with you. What you can explain without it is what you have learnt.
